title: Designing the perfect assessment system, part 4: slimming down the curriculum
author: Daisy Christodoulou
summary: In part four of her series on curriculum and assessment, Christodoulou takes apart the popular call to slim down the curriculum and teach fewer concepts in greater depth. She argues the slogan is so abstract that it justifies opposite practices, and that it is right in one respect and wrong in two. It is right for fundamentals such as number bonds, the letter-sound code and sentence structure, where primary curricula should go slow to go fast. It is wrong for reading comprehension, which depends on breadth of vocabulary and background knowledge, and wrong because concepts are themselves content, so reducing primary content implies increasing it at secondary. Her conclusion is that across-the-board reduction is wishful thinking that lowers standards unless the trade-off is accepted openly.
points: Slimming down is defensible only for fundamental concepts that need sustained practice, such as phonics, number bonds and basic sentence structure.
Reading comprehension needs breadth of vocabulary and knowledge rather than repeated strategy practice, so cutting history and geography undermines it.
Concepts are content: the best geologists have seen the most rocks, so skills cannot be separated from knowledge.
Cutting primary content is only sensible as a precursor to teaching more at secondary, not as a way to improve standards for free.
quotes: In debates about the curriculum, you’ll often hear that we need to "slim down" the curriculum. We need to focus on fewer concepts in greater depth. We need to stop racing superficially through a torrent of content and give students the chance to really understand what they are learning.

A number of researchers have noted that many East Asian maths curriculums have a slimmed down early years curriculum and high performance at the end of compulsory schooling. They go slow to go fast, because if you take the time to build solid foundations you make it easier to add an amazing superstructure.

The biggest change I would like to see in England at primary is a reduction in the grammar content. Currently, students are answering questions about modal verbs and fronted adverbials when they struggle to identify what a verb is. This is a classic example of running before you can walk - or, in a metaphor I’ve used many times before, training for a marathon by running a marathon.

Students don’t need tons of practice at using inference strategies. Instead, to be able to read well, what you need is a large vocabulary and background knowledge. When it comes to vocabulary, breadth matters more than depth.
Metaphors that pejoratively refer to curriculum content as “fat” and “clutter” miss this point. It’s not fat, it’s muscle. It’s not clutter, it’s substance.

I think this is wishful thinking. Yes, there are some parts of the primary curriculum where we should look to reduce content, but that’s generally as a precursor to being able to teach more content at secondary. If a curriculum reform leads to an across-the-board reduction in content, it’s likely to have lower standards.
